provenance: The artist; | Assistant to the artist, name and date unknown | Fraenkel Gallery, San Francisco, 1981 | Sotheby's Los Angeles, Photographs, 16-17 February 1982, Sale 330A, Lot 268; | Acquired from the above by the present owners. | | Literature | Vogue France, "Portrait de Fleur", vol. 8, no. 4, 1 April 1927, p. 36; | Man Ray: Photographs 1920-1934 (Paris, 1934), p. 23; | cf. Steven Manford, Behind the Photo: 42 Man Ray Stamps (Paris, 2008), n.p. (ill. stamps) | | Note | Man Ray's Magnolia Blossom is a striking example of the artist's ability to transform a simple natural form into a study of luminous elegance and modernist precision. Taken in 1926, the image features a single, curvaceous bloom, presented in a fluted vase placed on the seat of a café chair. The flower is captured at the moment when its satiny petals unfurl in the sunlight to reveal the tightly coiled carpels at its center. | | Magnolia Blossom was originally published as a full-page reproduction in the April 1927 issue of Vogue France and marks the notable inclusion of photography in the magazine's 'Art and Decoration' section, which duly credits Man Ray for the image. In the Vogue spread, Man Ray's signature appears at the lower right corner of the reproduced print. Over his long career, Man Ray chose to crop the negative of Magnolia in various ways as well as print it in both vertical and horizontal formats. Notably, the cropping in Vogue is very similar to that of the present work. | | The accompanying text dubs Man Ray as "Le Portraitiste des Choses" (the Portraitist of Things) - a subtly surrealist interpretation of a work that veers toward classicism. The caption also emphasizes the controlled harmony and beauty of the image ("presque impudique à force de splendeur" - almost immodest in its splendor). It is this quality which prompted the closing description of Magnolia as "plus pathétiques que la nature même" – more poignant than nature itself. | | Magnolia Blossom was one of Man Ray's favorite images from his robust and hyper-creative body of work made during the 1920s. In 1934, he published the book Man Ray: Photographs 1920-1934 – the first survey of his most important works to date – and selected it for inclusion. Made within the same few years that he created his most daring photographs, such as Le Violin d'Ingres (1924), Noire et blanche (1926), and his many extraordinary Rayographs, Magnolia Blossom exemplifies Man Ray's simultaneous engagement with classical motifs. Shifting subtly between abstraction and representation, this work conveys a vitality, lushness, and optimism that continues to captivate viewers. | | The present print was executed on paper with a silvery cast and was likely printed before 1940. The presence of two posthumous stamps, M28 and M30, indicates that the verso of the mount was stamped after Man Ray's death in 1976. At the time of this writing, the identity of the artist's assistant to whom Man Ray gifted this work remains unknown. Notably in the late 1970s, owners of Man Ray prints often approached the Estate and asked it to authenticate a photograph, which the Estate verified with posthumous stamps. This very special example of Magnolia Blossom has been carefully preserved and enjoyed by Lily Tomlin and Jane Wagner for more than forty years.

provenance: LA Louver, Los Angeles; | Acquired directly from the above by the present owners. | | Lot Essay | In 1986, Hockney began experimenting with the photocopier as a new medium for printmaking. This innovative process significantly shaped his creative output in the months that followed. Hockney once remarked, "I love new mediums... I think mediums can turn you on, they can excite you; they always let you do something in a different way. Even if you take the same subject, if you draw it in a different way, or if you are forced to simplify it—to make it bold because it is too finicky—I like that." | | By transforming the photocopier, an everyday office staple of the 1980s, into an accessible and dynamic artistic tool, Hockney redefined perceptions of the machine's potential. While many artists have hesitated to embrace emerging technologies, Hockney has consistently evolved alongside them, always adapting his printmaking to incorporate new technological possibilities, as demonstrated in this work.

provenance: Estate of Paul Outerbridge, Jr., 1976; | G. Ray Hawkins Gallery, Los Angeles; | Acquired from the above by the present owners in 1991. | | Literature | LIFE, vol. 9, no. 24, 9 December 1940, p. 59; | Elaine Dines, ed., Paul Outerbridge: A Singular Aesthetic, Photographs & Drawings 1921-1941, A Catalogue Raisonné (Santa Barbara, 1981), no. 502. | | Note | "So you think you'd like to photograph in color! Well, there's no reason why you shouldn't, but you'll have to take certain things into consideration." Thus begins Paul Outerbridge, Jr.'s seminal book Photographing in Color (1940), the definitive text on commercially available color printing processes. Although color photography was no longer a brand-new technology, it had yet to become frequently utilized in most photography circles. Through this exhaustive how-to manual, Outerbridge sought to demystify color printing processes. | | At a time when most photographers were still working in black and white, Outerbridge began experimenting with a variety of color processes as early as 1929. Indeed, he has long been credited as one of the first American photographers to embrace color printing as a serious artistic choice. In particular, Outerbridge committed himself to mastering the complex three-color Carbro (carbon-bromide) process. This method was labor-intensive, expensive, and technically demanding, but it produced extraordinarily rich, stable, and luminous color. "Each process has its distinct advantages, disadvantages, and techniques," Outerbridge acknowledged. "But the most time-consuming, the most temperamental, and the process capable of rendering the most beautiful results, in the opinion of most color workers, is Carbro." (Photographing in Color, p. 8). | | Throughout the 1930s, coloration became increasingly central in the advertising world. Outerbridge rightly credited the commercial trades for heightening the demand for color imagery and creating practical methods to achieve it. As American consumer culture expanded, companies sought to produce visual ad campaigns that simultaneously conveyed sophistication and captured the public's attention. Due in part to his technical mastery of the Carbro process, Outerbridge became a leading commercial photographer known for producing detailed, meticulously crafted imagery for magazines and national brands. | | The present work illustrates an advertisement created for A&P's 'Eight O'Clock Coffee' brand. Outerbridge staged an engaging domestic scene with a husband and wife at their breakfast table. His carefully crafted composition elevated the quotidian act of drinking one's morning coffee to an alluring and polished experience. This Carbro print was first reproduced in an A&P ad that ran in LIFE magazine in December 1940 – the same year that he published Photographing in Color as well as achieved his greatest commercial successes. Outerbridge's work in the field paved the way for subsequent champions of color photography as the practice slowly amassed popularity throughout the 20th Century. Through the end of his life, it remained his medium of choice. "In black and white you suggest," Outerbridge reminds us. "In color you state."

provenance: Fraenkel Gallery, San Francisco; | Acquired from the above by the present owners in 1980. | | Literature | John Gruen, 'Showing It Like It Is', World Journal Tribune, 26 February 1967, p. 31; | David Vestal, 'New Documents', Infinity, April 1967, p. 16; | Doon Arbus and Marvin Israel, eds. Diane Arbus (Aperture, 1972), no. 43; | Peter Galassi, American Photography 1890-1965 (New York: The Museum of Modern Art, 1995), p. 246; | Diane Arbus Revelations (New York, 2003), p. 102; | Intersections: Photographs and Videos from the National Gallery of Art and the Corcoran Gallery of Art (National Gallery of Art, Washington, 2016-2017), n.p.; | Sarah Hermanson Meister, Arbus, Friedlander, Winogrand: New Documents, 1967 (New York: The Museum of Modern Art, 2017), cover, pp. 53, 132, 152, 158. | | Note | During the 1963 holiday season, Diane Arbus took this double portrait of a teenage couple at Hudson and West 10th Streets, near her own home on Charles Street in Greenwich Village. Typical of her photographic practice at this time, she often stationed herself in a public area – Washington Square Park and Central Park were favorite destinations – so that she could observe the wide variety of people moving through the city. When she was particularly struck by a person or group, she might find the courage to approach them and ask if she could take their picture. | | In this instance, Arbus photographed a pair of kids who are likely not more than fifteen years old. At first glance, they seem more mature since their outfits would be appropriate for a couple twice their age. The girl wears a conservative knee-length coat with too-short sleeves, a patterned dress, sheer black stockings, and incongruously hip shoes. Her slightly mussed flip hairdo had received a shellacking of hairspray before she ventured out. After looking at her for a moment, a viewer may notice that she appears to have a black eye, probably the effect of a shadow falling across her face, but also possibly genuine. | | The boy strives to look grown-up and manly in his car coat, shirt and tie, narrow-legged trousers, and leather dress shoes. The front swoop of his ducktail hairstyle has partially fallen on his forehead on this chilly day. He stands a few inches taller than she is and proprietarily clutches her shoulder with his hand. In contrast, her single visible hand hangs limply at her side, indicating that she may be less invested in their relationship than he is. | | Diane Arbus once admitted, 'I work from awkwardness. By that I mean I don't like to arrange things. If I stand in front of something, instead of arranging it, I arrange myself.' (Aperture 1972, p. 12) One of Arbus's key strengths as a photographer was her ability to see her subjects for what they were, rather than directing them into a certain position or trying to elicit a particular emotional reaction. Awkwardness takes many forms in this portrait: their ill-fitting clothing, strained poses, and glances that look in different directions (his, tellingly, away from the camera) all speak to their discomfiture, much of which can be chalked up to typical teenage gawkiness and their liminal states of still-becoming. | | Arbus also emphasized awkwardness through her compositional choices, such as her camera angle that subtly peers down on the couple, making their heads appear a size too large for their slender bodies and foreshortened legs. This slightly elevated viewpoint also succeeds in throwing off the balance of the straight lines throughout the composition. The triangular sliver of doorway at the left edge of the frame tips away from the pair; the sloping line of the building's foundation stones makes the background feel topsy-turvy; and each of the wobbly horizontal lines of the brick wall suggest that this slice of sidewalk is not a stable, orderly space. | | Teenage Couple, Hudson Street remains one of Arbus's most recognizable works. Lifetime prints of this portrait are extremely rare, and only two have come to auction in the past 25 years. A print with a similar image size and a later printing date (1967-1970 according to the Estate of Diane Arbus) sold for $209,000 in March 2015. Another print with a larger image size and later printing date has appeared at auction twice – most notably when is sold for $271,203 in March 2019. | | Examples of this image are in the following collections: The Metropolitan Museum of Art (2005.493.3), The Museum of Modern Art (445.1973), and the Whitney Museum of American Art (P.2011.33), all in New York; as well as the National Gallery of Art, Washington D.C. provenance: Fraenkel Gallery, San Francisco; | Acquired from the above by the present owners in 1981. | | Note | In 1976, photography dealer Harry Lunn approached Gerd Sander—founder of the Washington, D.C.-based Sander Gallery and the grandson of photographer August Sander—about making a limited-edition portfolio of Lisette Model's work since her prints were not readily available for sale. As a magazine photographer turned teacher, Model did not have a stockpile of saleable work at this moment in her career. This portfolio presented a dozen of her most poignant, astringent, and pithy photographs, thus introducing Model to a broader audience and allowing her work to be acquired by a wider range of photography collectors.

artwork_title: Lily Tomlin as 'Trudy' (in 'The Search for Signs of Intelligent Life in the Universe')
provenance: Gift from the photographer to the present owners | | Note | Annie Leibovitz's photograph captures Lily Tomlin as Trudy the Bag Lady, one of the wholly unique female characters in The Search for Signs of Intelligent Life in the Universe. Jane Wagner wrote this one-woman stage production, which debuted on Broadway in 1985 and epitomizes Tomlin and Wagner's lifelong collaboration in both work and life. The play earned a multitude of awards, including the 1986 Tony for Best Actress in a Play, an Outer Critics Circle award, a special citation from the New York Drama Critics' Circle, and a Drama Desk Award for 'Unique Theatrical Experience'. The film version was released in 1991, bringing Tomlin and Wagner's magical cast of characters to a world-wide audience.
